chief_complaint: shortness of breath, chest pain, and rapid heartbeat after childbirth
hpi_details: A 31-year-old female presents with shortness of breath, chest pain, and rapid heartbeat after childbirth. Symptoms have become progressively worse.
ideas: She thinks her racing heart and breathlessness are just severe exhaustion and panic attacks caused by newborn sleep deprivation.
concerns: She is terrified that she might faint and drop her baby, or that something will happen to her and leave her newborn without a mother.
expectations: She hopes to get blood tests and a heart check today to confirm she is safe, along with medication that is safe to take while breastfeeding.

investigation_events.title: Transthoracic echocardiogram
investigation_events.availability_message: The transthoracic echocardiogram report is now available.

results.value: Dilated left ventricle with severe global hypokinesia; LVEF 30%; no significant valvular disease

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Peripartum Cardiomyopathy is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

This presentation requires urgent evaluation for heart failure and alternative life-threatening postpartum diagnoses. Echocardiography is essential for suspected peripartum cardiomyopathy; evaluation for pulmonary embolism should be guided by clinical probability and appropriate imaging rather than performed routinely.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: shortness of breath, chest pain, and rapid heartbeat after childbirth
Key HPI features: A 31-year-old female presents with shortness of breath, chest pain, and rapid heartbeat after childbirth, with progressive symptoms.
Objective/Exam findings: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Peripartum Cardiomyopathy.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Peripartum Cardiomyopathy.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Pulmonary embolism without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Breathlessness at rest, orthopnoea, or chest pain in the peripartum period.
management_principles: Urgently assess for heart failure and obtain echocardiography; evaluate pulmonary embolism when clinical probability warrants appropriate imaging
Treat acute heart failure and select guideline-directed therapy with obstetric/cardiology input, accounting for pregnancy and lactation status
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

teaching.one_liner: Heart failure appearing late in pregnancy or in the months after delivery — easily dismissed as normal postpartum tiredness.
red_flags: Breathlessness at rest, orthopnoea, or chest pain in the peripartum period

must_ask.say: How many weeks pregnant are you, or how long ago did you deliver?
Do you get breathless lying flat? How many pillows do you use?
Is this more breathlessness than you'd expect, compared with your other pregnancies?
Have your ankles or legs been swelling?
Have you had high blood pressure, headaches, or swelling in your hands and face?

must_ask.objective: Support at home with the baby
must_ask.say: Who is helping you at home with the baby?

history.answer: Ever since I gave birth two weeks ago, I have been getting very short of breath, my heart races constantly, and my chest feels tight.
It started gradually about a week after my delivery and has become progressively worse over the past several days.
The breathlessness used to only happen when I walked to the kitchen, but now I feel winded even while sitting resting or nursing my baby.
It is constant throughout the day and never completely goes away. I have never had any breathing troubles like this before.
Yes, whenever I lie flat on my back I feel like I am suffocating, so I have to prop myself up with three pillows to sleep.
Two nights ago I woke up gasping for air and had to sit upright by the open window for twenty minutes before I could breathe again.
Any kind of walking or lifting the baby makes it worse, and sitting upright gives me a little relief. Cold air, dust, and foods do not affect it.
No, I have not noticed any high-pitched wheezing or whistling sounds when I breathe.
I have a dry, irritating cough that gets worse when I lie down, but I have not had any phlegm or fever.
It is a dull, uncomfortable tightness across the center of my chest when my heart races, not a sharp stabbing pain when I breathe in.
Yes, my heart feels like it is pounding and racing out of my chest almost all the time. I feel lightheaded when standing up quickly, but I have not fainted.
No, I have never coughed up blood.
Both of my feet and ankles have puffed up significantly over the past week, and I have actually gained about three kilograms since leaving the hospital.
No, the swelling is even on both sides, neither calf is painful or red, and I have not been on any long flights or bedridden.
I do feel fatigued and worn out, but I have not noticed pale skin, and I only have normal postpartum spotting with no heavy bleeding or black stools.
No, I do not have any numbness or tingling in my fingers or lips, and this is not just nervousness or stress.
I delivered a healthy baby boy two weeks ago via an uncomplicated normal vaginal delivery.
During my pregnancy I had mild tiredness, but this shortness of breath is completely different and far more severe than anything I felt while pregnant.
No, I have had no severe headaches, no blurry vision or seeing spots, and no pain under my right ribs. My blood pressure was normal during prenatal visits.
My husband took two weeks of paternity leave and my mother is staying with us, so they are helping me take care of the newborn.
I thought my body was just crashing from severe sleep deprivation and panic attacks while adjusting to caring for a newborn.
I'm terrified that I might black out and drop my baby on the floor, or that I won't survive to watch him grow up.
I'm hoping you can check my heart and run some tests today to reassure me I'm okay, and give me something safe while I'm nursing.
I have always been healthy and have never been diagnosed with high blood pressure, heart problems, asthma, or diabetes.
I had no prior surgeries or hospital admissions other than giving birth to my baby two weeks ago.
I only take over-the-counter prenatal vitamins and iron supplements that my obstetrician recommended. No other medications.
I do not have any known allergies to medicines or foods.
I have never smoked cigarettes in my life.
I used to have an occasional glass of wine socially, but I stopped completely when I became pregnant and have not had a drop since.
I work as an elementary school teacher, currently on maternity leave, and I live in an apartment with my husband and baby. There is no dust or mold at home.
There is no family history of heart failure, sudden death, blood clots, or lung disease.
My last period was before this pregnancy about ten months ago. I am currently exclusively breastfeeding and we have not resumed sexual intercourse.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 130/84 mmHg, pulse 106 beats per minute, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 93% on room air, body temperature 36.7°C.
Tachypneic at rest with mild accessory muscle use; no perioral cyanosis or digital clubbing noted.
Conjunctivae are pink and non-pale; sclerae are anicteric.
Elevated jugular venous distension approximately 4 cm above the sternal angle at 45 degrees.
Percussion notes are resonant bilaterally with mild dullness at the bilateral lung bases.
Bilateral fine inspiratory crackles over the lower lung bases; no wheezing or rhonchi heard.
Tachycardic rhythm with an audible third heart sound (S3 gallop); no significant murmurs or pericardial friction rub.
Bilateral symmetrical 2+ pitting edema over both ankles and pretibial areas.
No focal calf swelling, localized erythema, warmth, or tenderness bilaterally.
